accuracy.evidence: Barriers (intact skin, nasal mucus and hairs, tears with lysozyme, stomach acid), phagocytes engulfing pathogens, lymphocytes making antigen-specific antibodies, memory cells giving a faster and larger secondary response, vaccines containing a weakened, inactivated or partial pathogen (or instructions for one part), and antibiotics acting on bacteria but not viruses were checked against the NHS vaccination pages, UKHSA Green Book chapter 1, BBC Bitesize KS3 defence against pathogens and OpenStax Biology 2e chapter 42. The doubling numbers are exact: 2 to 8 in 40 minutes and 5 to 40 in an hour at one split per 20 minutes. Graph shapes are labelled as a model, with the primary peak near two weeks and the secondary within days.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented child misconceptions about infection and immunity: germs that get in stay the same number (doubling scene and its prediction), one antibody fights every germ (the wrong-tip antibody is refused naming both shapes), you get just as ill a second time (the graph question refuses Second time), a vaccine is a medicine or gives you the disease (prediction, Ava's why-question and two challenge slips) and antibiotics cure a cold (challenge slip abx). Putting stomach acid on the eyes or tears on the nose is refused with each barrier's real job.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagimmune is about this topic's own mechanism in layers: four barrier doors plus a cut to plaster, a blood vessel where germs double per 20-minute tick while a white blood cell is dragged to swallow them, shape-matched Y antibodies on three germs, a primary-versus-secondary antibody graph, and a vaccinated-versus-unvaccinated comparison. It shares no mechanic with 493 Hygiene: washing away germs (flagsoap, spreading germs by touch and handwashing) or 738 Bones and muscles; the gate measures it under the 30 percent shingle limit against every other lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is met in the lab before the text confirms it: the learner sees 2 germs become 4 then 8 before the DONE line names doubling, finds that only the matching tips stick before the key-and-lock rule is stated, watches the second curve rise in days with a green Well band before being asked which time they were ill, and sees Ava stay well and Ben fall ill before choosing why. The vaccine must be given before the germ (refused otherwise), which makes the order of protection concrete.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: 'It stays at 2' (the clock doubles them), 'Yes, antibodies stop any germ' (wrong tips are refused), 'You get just as ill again' (the second curve and Well band), and 'A medicine that kills germs' for what is in a vaccine (Ava's vaccine contains no medicine and she still makes antibodies). The reveal line repeats the learner's own pick against the answer.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating questions checked in the browser with a script that clicks wrong options: each wrong option carries its own slip tag with a specific message: door (names what mucus, acid and tears each do), wait (5 germs become 40 in an hour), any (one key, one lock), same (memory cells within days), cure and disease (what a vaccine holds), abx (antibiotics kill bacteria, colds are viruses). Right answers restate the fact with a tick.

readability.evidence: Learner kid text measures FK grade 4.1 against a 6.5 limit, with short sentences and the precise words introduced in context: white blood cells, antibodies, memory cells, vaccine, bacteria, viruses. Adult text is 9.5 against 9.5 and names pathogen, phagocyte, lymphocyte, antigen and lysozyme. Lab scene text is one to three short sentences; card labels are one to three words.

no_filler.evidence: Kid paragraphs each do one job: barriers, germs that get in and phagocytes, antibodies with first and second responses, vaccines and antibiotics. Adult paragraphs give the two lines of defence with sources, then the named slips about vaccines and antibiotics, then what the lab does. The content gate finds no filler phrase and the explanation is under the 12 percent overlap limit against every lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 360 px phone screenshots in light and dark for all five scenes before and after Show me: the body box and four guard cards sit side by side with door labels clear of the head and arms, the blood vessel shows 8 germs in one row with the clock button beside the white blood cell, the three germs and three antibody cards fit one row each, the 40-day graph labels sit above the curve, and the two mini graphs with vaccine and germ markers fit under Ava and Ben with three answer boxes below.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag has a labelled button twin: one button per way in for the current guard card, a plaster button, Wait 20 minutes and Swallow a germ, one button per remaining antibody naming its tips and the germ, Germ gets in and Same germ again, First time and Second time, Vaccine to Ava or Ben, Germ reaches them, and one per reason. The canvas aria-label carries each scene description and every piece of feedback, right and wrong carry tick and cross marks as well as colour, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
